# A shower is a needle {#sec-axial-source}

@sec-event-moments compressed the *kernel* over a block and summed the source
exactly. This chapter does the opposite: it compresses the *source* and leaves
the kernel alone. The two are duals, and which one to spend on is a question
about the event, not about the method — so the chapter opens with what the
stored showers actually look like, and only then chooses.

The answer is that an electron shower is a needle with a nearly uniform
azimuth, and that both facts can be used without any fitting, any training and
any generated photon.

## What the stored showers look like {#sec-axial-shape}

`scripts/probe_shower_axis.py` takes the source contract of
@sec-source-contract, builds the photon-weighted principal axis of the emission
points, and reports the event in that frame. Six events of the stored
$100\,\mathrm{GeV}$ sample, with the spread of the six in the right column:

| quantity | event 5 | across events 0–5 |
|---|---:|---|
| longitudinal RMS | $1.23\,\mathrm m$ | $1.06$–$1.38$ |
| transverse RMS | $0.065\,\mathrm m$ | $0.062$–$0.072$ |
| aspect ratio | $19{:}1$ | $15$–$22$ |
| $\rho$, 99th percentile | $0.37\,\mathrm m$ | $0.37$–$0.42$ |
| the same as an angle at $25.7\,\mathrm m$ | $14\,\mathrm{mrad}$ | $14$–$16$ |
| residual emission time $\tau$, 99th percentile | $0.26\,\mathrm{ns}$ | $0.25$–$0.34$ |
| azimuthal anisotropy about the axis | $0.027$ | $0.017$–$0.068$ |

Three things in that table are worth reading carefully, because two of them
invite a simplification that the numbers do not support.

**The needle is real.** Nineteen to one, and the transverse spread is
$14\,\mathrm{mrad}$ seen from the nearest module. Whatever else is true, the
transverse coordinates are not where the information is.

**The emission time is not just $z/c_0$.** The median residual is $0.9\,$ps,
which invites dropping $\tau$ altogether. But the tail runs to $6.5\,\mathrm{ns}$
and a thousandth of the light is more than $0.9\,\mathrm{ns}$ late. The point
is moot in the end, because $\tau$ is free: it enters the projection as a
factor $e^{i\omega\tau}$ and adds no dimension to any table. A variable that
costs nothing should not be approximated.

**The emission direction is not narrow.** $\langle\mathbf u\cdot\hat{\mathbf a}
\rangle=0.87$ looks collimated until the tail is read: one per cent of the
light goes *backwards*, at $\cos<-0.41$. The angular variable needs real
resolution. It is the cone cosine that is nearly free, at $0.749\pm0.025$.

The correlations are stable from shower to shower to $\pm0.02$:
$\mathrm{corr}(z,\cos\theta)=-0.07$, $\mathrm{corr}(z,\tau)=+0.14$, and
$\mathrm{corr}(\cos\theta,\tau)=-0.33$. The last is the strongest thing in the
event — late light leaves sideways — and it is exactly what a source described
by separate profiles in $z$, in angle and in time would destroy.

## The reduction is an identity, not a fit {#sec-axial-identity}

Put the axis along $z$ and write the kernel's angular factor with the addition
theorem *in that frame*:

$$
P_\ell(\widehat{\mathbf r}\cdot\mathbf u)=\frac{4\pi}{2\ell+1}
\sum_m Y^{\mathrm R}_{\ell m}(\widehat{\mathbf r})\,Y^{\mathrm R}_{\ell m}(\mathbf u).
$$ {#eq-axis-addition}

Everything belonging to the source then separates from everything belonging to
the receiver, and the response of a source cut into cells is

$$
\boxed{
N(\omega)=\sum_\ell\frac{4\pi}{2\ell+1}\sum_m\sum_{\rm cells}
A_{\ell m}(\text{cell},\omega)\,M_\ell(r,\omega)\,
Y^{\mathrm R}_{\ell m}(\widehat{\mathbf r}),}
$$ {#eq-axial-response}

$$
A_{\ell m}(\text{cell},\omega)=\sum_{i\in\text{cell}}Q_i\,P_\ell(\mu_{C,i})\,
Y^{\mathrm R}_{\ell m}(\mathbf u_i)\,e^{i\omega t_i}.
$$ {#eq-axial-channels}

No approximation has been made yet. The compression is entirely in where the
two sums are cut, and the frame is what makes the cut cheap: keeping only
$m=0$ **is** the average over the azimuth of the emission direction about the
axis, which reduces the source to $L_q+1$ channels instead of $(L_q+1)^2$.
Keeping $|m|\le M$ restores the leading azimuthal correlation at

$$
N_{\rm ch}=(L_q+1)(2M+1)-M(M+1)
$$ {#eq-axial-channel-count}

channels: $33$ at $M=0$, $277$ at $M=4$ and $1089$ in full, for $L_q=32$. A
shower is azimuthally symmetric in distribution but not in any one
realisation, so $M$ is measured rather than assumed.

::: {.callout-important title="The emission time must not be rebuilt from the cell"}
An element moved to a cell centre changes its *propagation*. It must not change
when it radiated. The first version of this code stored the residual time
$\tau_i=t_i-t_0-z_i/c_0$ against its own $z_i$ while the response supplied the
front phase $e^{i\omega z_j/c_0}$ of the cell — which silently shifts the
emission by $(z_j-z_i)/c_0$, two radians per metre at
$\omega=0.6\,\mathrm{ns^{-1}}$. On two elements a metre apart the reconstructed
phase was wrong by $\pm2.0$ rad and the answer by a factor of three.

The cure is to store the absolute phase $e^{i\omega(t_i-t_{\rm ref})}$ from the
element's own time and drop the front factor entirely, so that the only thing
the move approximates is the propagation. Equivalently one may keep the front
factor and use $\tau_{ij}=t_i-t_0-z_j/c_0$ against the *cell's* $z_j$. A test
pins the identity down, because this is the kind of error that shows up as a
plausible few per cent rather than as a crash.
:::

## Where the light goes on the grid {#sec-axial-deposit}

Elements are spread over the surrounding cell centres with trilinear weights,
which satisfy

$$
\sum_j W_j(\mathbf x_i)=1,\qquad
\sum_j W_j(\mathbf x_i)\,\mathbf X_j=\mathbf x_i,
$$ {#eq-cic}

so both the photon count and its first spatial moment survive the move. Both
hold to machine precision on the stored event; nearest-cell assignment holds
the first and misplaces the second by about a tenth of a cell.

That is worth a factor of ten in practice. Against the element sum, refining
the cell:

| cell | $\omega=0$ | $\omega=0.3$ | $\omega=0.6$ |
|---:|---|---|---|
| $0.24\,\mathrm m$ | $1.11\times10^{-4}$ | $9.36\times10^{-3}$ | $3.84\times10^{-2}$ |
| $0.12\,\mathrm m$ | $2.58\times10^{-5}$ $(+2.10)$ | $2.33\times10^{-3}$ $(+2.01)$ | $9.31\times10^{-3}$ $(+2.05)$ |
| $0.06\,\mathrm m$ | $5.93\times10^{-6}$ $(+2.12)$ | $5.65\times10^{-4}$ $(+2.04)$ | $2.38\times10^{-3}$ $(+1.97)$ |

The bracketed numbers are $\log_2$ of the ratio to the row above: second order,
at every frequency, not only at $\omega=0$ where smoothness is easiest. The
nearest-cell rule is first order and stalls near $10^{-2}$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Two errors that hid behind each other"}
That clean second order only appeared after two separate mistakes were removed,
and both are worth recording because each looked like the other.

The first was a transverse grid sized to the 99th percentile of $\rho$, with
everything beyond it clipped into the outermost cells. The tail of $\rho$
reaches $2.3\,\mathrm m$, so one per cent of the light was being moved by
$1.8\,\mathrm m$ — five radians at the top frequency. The error sat at
$1.2\times10^{-2}$ and refused to converge in anything. Cells of a fixed
physical size with sparse storage cure it: empty cells cost nothing, so there
is never a reason to clip a source tail.

The second was subtler. The element sum integrates each G4 step along its
chord with a Gauss rule and interpolates the emission time along it; the
projection was placing the step at its midpoint with its *start* time. On a
half-millimetre step that is nothing at $\omega=0$ — $4.9\times10^{-8}$ — and
$7.7\times10^{-3}$ at $\omega=0.6$, which is precisely where the convergence
was stalling. It was never the grid. When two routes are compared, a
difference in how they treat one element wears the costume of a method error.
:::

## The run {#sec-axial-run}

One stored event, the whole array, the whole frequency window: $L_q=32$,
$M=4$, cells of $0.12\,\mathrm m$, $41$ frequencies to
$\omega=0.5\,\mathrm{ns^{-1}}$, $576$ modules at $25.7$–$317.3\,\mathrm m$.
The compact source is $4\,935$ cells $\times$ $277$ channels $\times$ $41$
frequencies.

The reference is the same kernel summed element by element, at six control
modules. **What follows is therefore a median over six modules, not the
accuracy of all $576$**: the approximate answer is computed everywhere, the
exact one is not.

| | median | worst of the six | on the summed signal |
|---|---|---|---|
| charge, order $1$ | $2.4\times10^{-3}$ | $6.9\times10^{-3}$ | $6.9\times10^{-3}$ |
| charge, order $\ge2$ | $4.3\times10^{-4}$ | $1.8\times10^{-3}$ | $1.8\times10^{-3}$ |
| spectrum at $\omega=0.25$, $\ge2$ | $4.5\times10^{-3}$ | $1.4\times10^{-2}$ | — |
| spectrum at $\omega=0.50$, $\ge2$ | $1.7\times10^{-2}$ | $1.8\times10^{-1}$ | — |

Charge is comfortably inside a per cent. The spectrum degrades with frequency,
and the refinement below says exactly which knob it answers to.

### Which knob the error answers to {#sec-axial-refine}

One setting changed at a time, everything else held, $\ge2$ component, median
over the same six modules:

| change | cells | channels | $\omega=0$ | $\omega=0.25$ | $\omega=0.5$ |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|---|
| baseline: $M=4$, cell $0.12$ | $4\,935$ | $277$ | $4.3\times10^{-4}$ | $4.5\times10^{-3}$ | $1.7\times10^{-2}$ |
| $M=2$ | $4\,935$ | $159$ | $1.6\times10^{-3}$ | $1.1\times10^{-2}$ | $4.3\times10^{-2}$ |
| $M=8$ | $4\,935$ | $489$ | $1.5\times10^{-4}$ | $1.5\times10^{-3}$ | $7.3\times10^{-3}$ |
| cell $0.03\,\mathrm m$ | $32\,861$ | $277$ | $4.2\times10^{-4}$ | $3.9\times10^{-3}$ | $1.6\times10^{-2}$ |
| transverse cell $0.03\,\mathrm m$ | $18\,231$ | $277$ | $4.3\times10^{-4}$ | $4.3\times10^{-3}$ | $1.7\times10^{-2}$ |
| four chord nodes instead of two | $4\,936$ | $277$ | $4.3\times10^{-4}$ | $4.5\times10^{-3}$ | $1.7\times10^{-2}$ |
| nearest-cell deposit | $1\,706$ | $277$ | $5.6\times10^{-4}$ | $1.1\times10^{-2}$ | $1.7\times10^{-2}$ |

The reading is unambiguous. **Only $M$ moves the answer.** Six-fold finer cells
change nothing; finer transverse cells change nothing; doubling the chord
quadrature changes nothing. At these settings the spatial grid is converged and
the azimuthal truncation is the whole of the remaining error, so the way to a
better answer is more $m$ channels, not a finer mesh — which is the opposite of
what the frequency behaviour alone would suggest, and is why the refinement is
run one knob at a time.

### Time bins {#sec-axial-bins}

A spectrum that agrees at four frequencies can still misplace an edge, so the
bins are produced and compared as bins. Getting them right took two corrections,
and the second was an outright error.

A frequency grid of spacing $\Delta\omega$ reconstructs times only out to about
$\pi/\Delta\omega$. Light reaches the control modules at $116$ to
$1439\,\mathrm{ns}$, so binning from $t=0$ on a $300\,\mathrm{ns}$ window put
the far modules entirely outside it. Each module's bins are now measured from
its own geometric arrival $r/v$, and the grid is $81$ frequencies — a horizon of
$503\,\mathrm{ns}$ against a window of $480$.

::: {.callout-important title="A sign that both sides of a comparison hid"}
This repository transforms with $e^{+i\omega t}$, so moving the time origin to
$t_d$ requires multiplying the spectrum by $e^{-i\omega t_d}$. The first version
used $e^{+i\omega t_d}$, which does not bring the pulse back to zero — it pushes
it one arrival time further out. A unit pulse at $135\,\mathrm{ns}$ with the
origin at $120$ lands at $255\,\mathrm{ns}$ instead of $15$.

The comparison did not notice, because the compact route and the element sum
were multiplied by the same wrong factor and agreed with each other to a few
parts in a thousand in a window that contained almost nothing but ringing. The
agreement was real and meaningless. What gave it away was not the error
statistic but the *share of the signal* in the early window: a hundredth of a
per cent, where physics says most of the light arrives in the first tens of
nanoseconds.

The lesson is narrower than "check your signs". A quantity applied identically
to both sides of a comparison is invisible to that comparison, however careful
it is, and only an absolute statement about the answer — here, where the light
should be — can catch it.
:::

With the sign corrected, per control module, $10\,\mathrm{ns}$ bins, no
detector smearing:

| module distance, m | $25.7$ | $99.3$ | $144.3$ | $185.7$ | $233.6$ | $317.3$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| peak bin, ns after arrival | $15$ | $15$ | $15$ | $25$ | $25$ | $25$ |
| $\ge2$: largest bin error / peak | $4.0\text{e-}3$ | $1.5\text{e-}3$ | $1.7\text{e-}3$ | $6.7\text{e-}4$ | $1.2\text{e-}3$ | $6.0\text{e-}4$ |
| $\ge2$: integral over the window | $1.8\text{e-}3$ | $1.6\text{e-}3$ | $5.7\text{e-}4$ | $9.5\text{e-}5$ | $1.2\text{e-}4$ | $2.2\text{e-}4$ |
| $\ge2$: first $50\,\mathrm{ns}$ | $2.1\text{e-}3$ | $1.8\text{e-}3$ | $6.7\text{e-}4$ | $1.2\text{e-}4$ | $2.6\text{e-}4$ | $4.0\text{e-}4$ |
| $\ge2$: share of the signal there | $0.87$ | $0.88$ | $0.87$ | $0.78$ | $0.59$ | $0.65$ |
| order $1$: largest bin error / peak | $8.8\text{e-}3$ | $5.0\text{e-}3$ | $4.7\text{e-}3$ | $3.8\text{e-}3$ | $6.6\text{e-}3$ | $1.3\text{e-}3$ |
| order $1$: first $50\,\mathrm{ns}$ | $6.4\text{e-}3$ | $6.2\text{e-}3$ | $3.4\text{e-}3$ | $9.1\text{e-}4$ | $2.4\text{e-}3$ | $1.1\text{e-}2$ |

Every peak sits $15$–$25\,\mathrm{ns}$ after the geometric arrival, the early
window now carries $59$–$88\%$ of the $\ge2$ signal, and it is reproduced to
between $10^{-4}$ and $2\times10^{-3}$. The one entry that looks poor — order
$1$ at $317\,\mathrm m$, $1.1\times10^{-2}$ — is a module whose early share is
$-0.04$: there is no unscattered-adjacent light there at all and the window
holds ringing.

Negative bins are kept as computed and are the same on both sides: $0.4\%$ of
the mass for order $1$ and below $0.1\%$ for $\ge2$, in the element sum and in
the compact source alike. That is the finite frequency window, not the
representation.

## What it costs, and why that is the wrong number {#sec-axial-cost}

Per event, after the cache, for all $576$ modules at $41$ frequencies:

| stage | seconds |
|---|---:|
| read the file and apply the source contract | $0.2$ |
| compile the compact source | $190.6$ |
| apply, order $1$ | $993.8$ |
| apply, order $\ge2$ | $1012.1$ |
| unscattered order, closed form, all modules | $6.7$ |
| readout to time bins | $0.04$ |
| **total** | $2203$ |

That is $37$ minutes for one shower, against $11.6$ hours for the element sum
at the same settings — a factor of $19$, and useless. Nineteen times a number
that is far too large is still far too large, and the interesting question is
not the ratio but why both numbers are what they are.

The apply is $576\times4935\times277\times41=3.2\times10^{10}$ complex terms,
and it runs at $16$ million a second on hardware that does $10^9$. Profiling it
finds, in order: the spherical harmonics, the final contraction, a **pure
gather that expands $33$ radial moments into $277$ channels by duplication**,
and the spline. The gather is the clearest waste — the cached moment $M_\ell$
has no $m$ index and never needed one — and the two scattered orders repeat
every distance, direction and harmonic because they are computed in separate
passes.

Neither is a property of the method. Both are properties of how the sum was
written.

::: {.callout-important title="Reordering is not enough; not materialising is"}
The obvious repair is to contract the azimuthal channels first, so the degree
axis stays $33$ long, and to take both orders from one pass. Written that way
in numpy — `experimental/axial_blocked.py` — it agrees with the original to
$4\times10^{-15}$ and is **not faster**: $3.4\,\mathrm s$ per module against
$3.0$, measured on the stored event at full size.

The reason is worth stating, because it decides what to build. Removing the
gather does not remove the array: numpy still has to *materialise* something
indexed by (receiver, cell, degree, order, frequency) in order to contract it.
A fused loop does not. The whole of the available speed is in never forming the
intermediate at all, and that cannot be expressed in array operations.

So the reordering is necessary and worthless on its own. It pays only inside a
compiled kernel, where the $(r,b,\ell,o,w)$ quantity lives in registers and the
source array is read once per block of receivers instead of once per receiver.
:::

The same holds for the source compile. Of its $191\,\mathrm s$, the harmonics
are $7$ and the emission phases are under $1$; about $30$ go into building the
element $\times$ channel $\times$ frequency outer product and the rest into
moving it through a sparse product. The product never needs to exist: the
accumulation into one cell is a small matrix multiply of that cell's own
elements.

A compiled backend along these lines is in `experimental/axial_fast.py`, which
requires the optional `accelerate` extra. Its arithmetic is verified against
the route above — source coefficients to $6\times10^{-16}$, both scattered
orders to $4\times10^{-15}$, a rigid pose change to $6\times10^{-16}$ — and its
speed is not measured here, because this machine has no compiler for it. The
timings in this section are therefore the honest cost of the *unoptimised*
route, and the table above should be read as the thing to be replaced rather
than as the cost of the physics.

Peak resident memory for the run was $5.3\,\mathrm{GB}$, and the compact source
is $855\,\mathrm{MB}$ — $4935\times277\times41$ complex numbers. That is the
number to keep in mind when the word "compact" is used: the *cells* are sparse,
the channels and frequencies at each cell are not. The transport cache, by
contrast, is $6.6\,\mathrm{MB}$ and is built once per medium; a small cache
does not make a large source cheap to apply.

## A new pose, and an event the settings never saw {#sec-axial-transfer}

The transport cache does not know where the event is. A pose chosen *after* the
tables were built — rotated by $0.9$ rad, translated $60\,\mathrm m$, delayed
$25\,\mathrm{ns}$, with control modules now at $26$–$343\,\mathrm m$ — is
answered by the same cache, compiled in $178\,\mathrm s$, with charge errors of
$9.5\times10^{-4}$ (median) and $2.5\times10^{-3}$ (worst) for $\ge2$ and
$4.3\times10^{-3}$ / $1.2\times10^{-2}$ for order $1$.

Event $6$, read with every setting frozen from event $5$, gives
$3.5\times10^{-4}$ and $2.8\times10^{-3}$ for $\ge2$ — no worse than the event
the settings were chosen on, which is the only evidence that they were not
tuned to it.

## What this does not settle {#sec-axial-limits}

The reference throughout is the same kernel summed element by element. That
isolates the error of the source representation, which is what this chapter is
about, and it is not physics: the independent physical control of the $\ge2$
component that @sec-segment-limits asked for is still owed, and stacking a
measured representation on an unmeasured component would be a poor trade.

Nothing here establishes a *minimum* number of coefficients. @eq-axis-addition
gives the exact harmonic content of one cone; it says nothing about how few
numbers could describe a family of showers. Whether the
$(\text{cell},\ell m)$ array compresses further — and against which norm, since
a mode that is small in the source can be large in the response — is a
measurement that has not been made.

The receiver is still an isotropic point, one wavelength band, one medium. And
the frequency behaviour above is the behaviour of *this* representation: the
phase across a cell is a real scale, but it bounds a spatial projection, not
every conceivable scheme.
